title: Uttara's charioteer
hookLine: Prince Uttara boasts he'd beat the Kuru army if only he had a charioteer, and the dance teacher volunteers
carry: parthasarathy: god holds the reins when fear comes

cards: Cattle raiders. The Kauravas have heard that Kichaka is dead, and they come for King Virata's herds. The king has already ridden out to fight raiders on another side, taking Kanka, the cook and the herdsmen with him.
At home, among the women of the palace, sits his young son, Prince Uttara. And Uttara talks big. If I only had a charioteer, he says, I'd beat the whole Kuru army.
They'd look at me and wonder if I was Arjuna himself. The person he's talking about is standing a few feet away, in bangles.

teach.h: UTTARA SEES THE ARMY, AND RUNS
teach.b: Sairandhri speaks up: Brihannala once drove a chariot for Arjuna. Uttara is embarrassed, but he has no one else. The teacher fumbles the armor on purpose, and the palace women laugh.
Then the chariot rolls out, and Uttara sees the army: banners, elephants, Bhishma, Drona, Karna. His boast falls apart. He jumps down and runs.
Brihannala runs after him, braid flying, and some Kuru soldiers think: that runs like Arjuna. The teacher catches the prince, not to shame him but to steady him. Don't be afraid, he says, in effect.
You drive. I'll fight. At the shami tree Uttara unwraps the bundle and finds the great bow Gandiva.
Whose are these? And Brihannala tells him: I am Arjuna. Now hold that picture, because the epic will turn it around.
Soon, on the field of Kurukshetra, Arjuna himself will lose his nerve and let his bow slip, and his charioteer, Krishna, will steady him. That conversation is the Bhagavad Gita.
Many readers notice the echo: the man who says you drive, I'll fight, will soon need someone at the reins for him.
It's why Hindus love Krishna as Parthasarathy, Arjuna's charioteer, and temples in his name still draw crowds. The teaching: in Hindu devotion, God doesn't only watch from far above the battle.
God takes the reins beside the frightened. Today fear still makes us jump from the chariot. The epic's answer isn't shame.
It's someone who runs after you.

how: Retellings of the Virata book linger on Uttara's boast and flight and on Brihannala chasing him across the field, a scene that mixes comedy with the moment Arjuna is revealed.

o: the king of the Matsyas, father of Prince Uttara
the prince who boasts, then runs from the Kurus
the charioteer who once drove for Arjuna

games.q: the cattle raid — tap the pairs.
p: said Brihannala once drove for Arjuna
asked for cloths for their dolls

s: Parthasarathy is a name for Krishna as Arjuna's charioteer
Hindus worship him by that name: God at the reins for a frightened friend.
Brihannala ran after the prince across the field
braid flying, and some Kuru soldiers thought the runner moved like Arjuna.
Arjuna first revealed himself to King Virata
he told Prince Uttara, at the shami tree, before anyone else.

games.q: you're Brihannala. the prince you're driving has jumped from the chariot and is running away from the Kuru army. what do you do?
o: let him go and face the army alone.
run after him, bring him back, and let him drive while you fight.
throw off the disguise and call to the Kurus.
games.why: Arjuna chases him down, steadies him and gives him the reins, as Krishna will one day do for Arjuna.

practice: Many Hindu homes keep a picture of Krishna driving Arjuna's chariot. Feel your feet on the floor and bring to mind one thing you've been running from.

Breathing in, picture someone steady at the reins beside you: Krishna, if you pray to him, or someone who has steadied you before. Breathing out, let your hands rest, as if you could face it now, not alone.
If you pray, you can bring it to God in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Virata. The kingdom whose frightened prince learns, on a battlefield, who his dance teacher really is.

carryVoice: Your line: Parthasarathy: God holds the reins when fear comes. A boast, a run, and a teacher who ran after him. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Go-harana), the Kuru cattle raid, Uttara's boast and flight, Brihannala as charioteer, and the weapons recovered from the shami tree
